def clean_columns(df):
    rename_map = {
        "Sex": "sex",
        "Length": "length",
        "Diameter": "diameter",
        "Height": "height",
        "Whole weight": "whole_weight",
        "Whole weight.1": "whole_weight_1",
        "Whole weight.2": "whole_weight_2",
        "Shell weight": "shell_weight",
        "Rings": "rings",
        "id": "id",
        "Id": "id"
    }
    out = df.rename(columns=rename_map).copy()
    return out

train = clean_columns(train_raw)
test = clean_columns(test_raw)

required_train_cols = [
    "id", "sex", "length", "diameter", "height",
    "whole_weight", "whole_weight_1", "whole_weight_2",
    "shell_weight", "rings"
]

required_test_cols = [
    "id", "sex", "length", "diameter", "height",
    "whole_weight", "whole_weight_1", "whole_weight_2",
    "shell_weight"
]

missing_train = [c for c in required_train_cols if c not in train.columns]
missing_test = [c for c in required_test_cols if c not in test.columns]

if missing_train:
    raise ValueError(f"Missing columns in train.csv: {missing_train}")
if missing_test:
    raise ValueError(f"Missing columns in test.csv: {missing_test}")

print("Cleaned train columns:", train.columns.tolist())

Basic cleaning and validation¶

numeric_cols = [
    "length", "diameter", "height",
    "whole_weight", "whole_weight_1",
    "whole_weight_2", "shell_weight"
]

categorical_col = "sex"
target_col = "rings"

# Convert categorical to string just in case
train[categorical_col] = train[categorical_col].astype(str)
test[categorical_col] = test[categorical_col].astype(str)

# Coerce numeric columns
for col in numeric_cols + [target_col]:
    train[col] = pd.to_numeric(train[col], errors="coerce")

for col in numeric_cols:
    test[col] = pd.to_numeric(test[col], errors="coerce")

# Median imputation for any missing numeric values
for col in numeric_cols:
    train[col] = train[col].fillna(train[col].median())
    test[col] = test[col].fillna(train[col].median())

# Mode imputation for sex if needed
train[categorical_col] = train[categorical_col].fillna(train[categorical_col].mode().iloc[0])
test[categorical_col] = test[categorical_col].fillna(train[categorical_col].mode().iloc[0])

# Target must not be missing
train = train.dropna(subset=[target_col]).reset_index(drop=True)

print("Final test shape:", test.shape)

Define formulas¶

Baseline linear model is included only for comparison.¶

Assignment A.1 focuses on the two nonlinear models.¶

In [ ]:
linear_formula = (
    "rings ~ C(sex) + length + diameter + height + whole_weight + "
    "whole_weight_1 + whole_weight_2 + shell_weight"
)

# Nonlinear Model 1: Additive polynomial regression with quadratic terms
poly_formula = (
    "rings ~ C(sex) + length + diameter + height + whole_weight + whole_weight_1 + "
    "whole_weight_2 + shell_weight + "
    "I(length**2) + I(diameter**2) + I(height**2) + I(whole_weight**2) + "
    "I(whole_weight_1**2) + I(whole_weight_2**2) + I(shell_weight**2)"
)

# Nonlinear Model 2: Additive natural cubic spline regression
# df values are chosen to give flexibility without being overly unstable
spline_formula = (
    "rings ~ C(sex) + "
    "cr(length, df=5) + "
    "cr(diameter, df=5) + "
    "cr(height, df=4) + "
    "cr(whole_weight, df=5) + "
    "cr(whole_weight_1, df=4) + "
    "cr(whole_weight_2, df=4) + "
    "cr(shell_weight, df=4)"
)

print("Baseline linear formula:")
print(linear_formula)
print("\nPolynomial formula:")
print(poly_formula)
print("\nSpline formula:")
print(spline_formula)

rings ~ C(sex) + length + diameter + height + whole_weight + whole_weight_1 + whole_weight_2 + shell_weight

Polynomial formula:
rings ~ C(sex) + length + diameter + height + whole_weight + whole_weight_1 + whole_weight_2 + shell_weight + I(length**2) + I(diameter**2) + I(height**2) + I(whole_weight**2) + I(whole_weight_1**2) + I(whole_weight_2**2) + I(shell_weight**2)

Spline formula:
rings ~ C(sex) + cr(length, df=5) + cr(diameter, df=5) + cr(height, df=4) + cr(whole_weight, df=5) + cr(whole_weight_1, df=4) + cr(whole_weight_2, df=4) + cr(shell_weight, df=4)

Helper functions¶

In [ ]:
def rmsle(y_true, y_pred):
    y_true = np.asarray(y_true, dtype=float)
    y_pred = np.asarray(y_pred, dtype=float)
    y_pred = np.clip(y_pred, 0, None)
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean((np.log1p(y_true) - np.log1p(y_pred)) ** 2)))

def regression_metrics(y_true, y_pred):
    y_true = np.asarray(y_true, dtype=float)
    y_pred = np.asarray(y_pred, dtype=float)

    rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((y_true - y_pred) ** 2)))
    mae = float(np.mean(np.abs(y_true - y_pred)))

    ss_res = float(np.sum((y_true - y_pred) ** 2))
    ss_tot = float(np.sum((y_true - np.mean(y_true)) ** 2))
    r2 = float(1 - ss_res / ss_tot)

    return {
        "rmse": rmse,
        "mae": mae,
        "r2": r2,
        "rmsle": rmsle(y_true, y_pred)
    }

def cross_validate_formula(data, formula, n_splits=5, random_state=42):
    kf = KFold(n_splits=n_splits, shuffle=True, random_state=random_state)

    fold_rows = []

    for fold, (train_idx, valid_idx) in enumerate(kf.split(data), start=1):
        fold_train = data.iloc[train_idx].copy()
        fold_valid = data.iloc[valid_idx].copy()

        model = smf.ols(formula, data=fold_train).fit()
        preds = model.predict(fold_valid)

        mets = regression_metrics(fold_valid[target_col], preds)

        fold_rows.append({
            "fold": fold,
            "rmse": mets["rmse"],
            "mae": mets["mae"],
            "r2": mets["r2"],
            "rmsle": mets["rmsle"]
        })

    fold_df = pd.DataFrame(fold_rows)

    summary_df = pd.DataFrame([{
        "cv_rmse_mean": fold_df["rmse"].mean(),
        "cv_rmse_std": fold_df["rmse"].std(ddof=1),
        "cv_mae_mean": fold_df["mae"].mean(),
        "cv_r2_mean": fold_df["r2"].mean(),
        "cv_rmsle_mean": fold_df["rmsle"].mean(),
        "cv_rmsle_std": fold_df["rmsle"].std(ddof=1)
    }])

    return fold_df, summary_df

def fit_model_with_table(model_name, formula, data):
    model = smf.ols(formula, data=data).fit()
    fitted = model.predict(data)
    mets = regression_metrics(data[target_col], fitted)

    row = {
        "model": model_name,
        "n_obs": int(model.nobs),
        "df_model": float(model.df_model),
        "df_resid": float(model.df_resid),
        "r_squared": float(model.rsquared),
        "adj_r_squared": float(model.rsquared_adj),
        "aic": float(model.aic),
        "bic": float(model.bic),
        "f_statistic": float(model.fvalue),
        "f_pvalue": float(model.f_pvalue),
        "train_rmse": mets["rmse"],
        "train_mae": mets["mae"],
        "train_r2": mets["r2"],
        "train_rmsle": mets["rmsle"]
    }

    return model, row

def coefficient_table(model):
    tbl = model.summary2().tables[1].copy()
    tbl = tbl.reset_index().rename(columns={"index": "term"})
    return tbl

def diagnostic_summary_table(model, label):
    resid = model.resid
    exog = model.model.exog

    bp_test = het_breuschpagan(resid, exog)
    jb_stat, jb_pvalue, skewness, kurtosis = jarque_bera(resid)
    dw_stat = durbin_watson(resid)

    out = pd.DataFrame([{
        "model": label,
        "breusch_pagan_lm_stat": bp_test[0],
        "breusch_pagan_lm_pvalue": bp_test[1],
        "breusch_pagan_f_stat": bp_test[2],
        "breusch_pagan_f_pvalue": bp_test[3],
        "jarque_bera_stat": jb_stat,
        "jarque_bera_pvalue": jb_pvalue,
        "skewness": skewness,
        "kurtosis": kurtosis,
        "durbin_watson": dw_stat
    }])

    return out

def vif_table(model, top_n=None):
    exog = pd.DataFrame(model.model.exog, columns=model.model.exog_names).copy()

    # Remove intercept
    keep_cols = [c for c in exog.columns if c.lower() not in ("intercept", "const")]
    exog = exog[keep_cols]

    # Remove zero-variance columns if any
    exog = exog.loc[:, exog.nunique() > 1]

    rows = []
    for i, col in enumerate(exog.columns):
        vif_value = variance_inflation_factor(exog.values, i)
        rows.append({"term": col, "VIF": float(vif_value)})

    vif_df = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("VIF", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

    if top_n is not None:
        return vif_df.head(top_n)

    return vif_df

def make_effect_df(train_df, predictor, n_points=200):
    grid = np.linspace(train_df[predictor].min(), train_df[predictor].max(), n_points)

    base_row = {
        "sex": train_df["sex"].mode().iloc[0],
        "length": train_df["length"].median(),
        "diameter": train_df["diameter"].median(),
        "height": train_df["height"].median(),
        "whole_weight": train_df["whole_weight"].median(),
        "whole_weight_1": train_df["whole_weight_1"].median(),
        "whole_weight_2": train_df["whole_weight_2"].median(),
        "shell_weight": train_df["shell_weight"].median()
    }

    pred_df = pd.DataFrame([base_row] * n_points)
    pred_df[predictor] = grid
    return pred_df

def interpret_bp(p):
    return "No strong evidence of heteroscedasticity" if p > 0.05 else "Evidence of heteroscedasticity"

def interpret_jb(p):
    return "Residuals are closer to normality" if p > 0.05 else "Residuals depart from normality"

def interpret_dw(dw):
    if 1.5 <= dw <= 2.5:
        return "No strong evidence of autocorrelation"
    elif dw < 1.5:
        return "Possible positive autocorrelation"
    else:
        return "Possible negative autocorrelation"

Residual and diagnostic plots¶

In [ ]:
def diagnostic_plots(model, model_name, qq_sample_size=5000):
    fitted = model.fittedvalues
    resid = model.resid

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(14, 10))

    # Residuals vs fitted
    axes[0, 0].scatter(fitted, resid, alpha=0.25, s=12)
    axes[0, 0].axhline(0, color="red", linestyle="--")
    axes[0, 0].set_title(f"{model_name}: Residuals vs Fitted")
    axes[0, 0].set_xlabel("Fitted values")
    axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("Residuals")

    # Actual vs fitted
    axes[0, 1].scatter(model.model.endog, fitted, alpha=0.25, s=12)
    min_val = min(model.model.endog.min(), fitted.min())
    max_val = max(model.model.endog.max(), fitted.max())
    axes[0, 1].plot([min_val, max_val], [min_val, max_val], color="red", linestyle="--")
    axes[0, 1].set_title(f"{model_name}: Actual vs Fitted")
    axes[0, 1].set_xlabel("Actual Rings")
    axes[0, 1].set_ylabel("Fitted Rings")

    # Histogram of residuals
    axes[1, 0].hist(resid, bins=40, alpha=0.8)
    axes[1, 0].set_title(f"{model_name}: Residual Histogram")
    axes[1, 0].set_xlabel("Residual")
    axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("Frequency")

    # QQ plot using a sample for readability on large data
    qq_resid = resid
    if len(qq_resid) > qq_sample_size:
        qq_resid = qq_resid.sample(qq_sample_size, random_state=42)

    sm.qqplot(qq_resid, line="45", ax=axes[1, 1], fit=True)
    axes[1, 1].set_title(f"{model_name}: Q-Q Plot")

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

diagnostic_plots(poly_model, "Nonlinear Model 1: Polynomial")
diagnostic_plots(spline_model, "Nonlinear Model 2: Natural Cubic Spline")

Part C: Nonlinear Regression Analysis for the Abalone Rings Prediction Problem¶

(a) Building Two Nonlinear Models¶

In our Abalone dataset analysis collected from Kaggle, we were asked to construct and evaluate two nonlinear regression models. Our target variable was Rings, which was used to predict abalone age. The training dataset contained 90.615 observations and 10 variables, while the test dataset contained 60.411 observations and 9 variables. The first nonlinear model was an additive polynomial regression model. The response variable Rings was modeled as a function of Sex, all original quantitative predictors, and a quadratic term for each quantitative predictor. Polynomial regression extends linear regression by adding transformed versions of the original values, such as X^2, while the model remains linear in the unknown coefficients and can still be estimated with OLS. Here, the goal was not to force every predictor into a straight line relationship with Rings, but instead to follow the data to show whether curvature was present (Chesnaye et al., 2024). Our results showed that the polynomial model improved fit relative to the baseline linear model. The baseline linear model produced an R2 of 0.605587, a training RMSE of 1.994730, and a training RMSLE of 0.164916. By contrast, the polynomial model increased R2 to 0.630001, reduced training RMSE to 1.932006, and lowered training RMSLE to 0.160628. This means the nonlinear terms captured patterns that the baseline linear model could not represent. The ANOVA comparison between the linear and polynomial models further confirmed this improvement. When it comes to the test dataset, we have the metrics like F-statistics of 854.020615 with a p-value of 0.0, and this shows that the added quadratic terms significantly improved the model. The second nonlinear model was an additive natural cubic spline regression, which replaced straight line effects with smooth spline functions for each quantitative predictor while keeping the additive structure of the regression (James et al., 2023). The spline model produced the best overall performance, full training data has and R2 of 0.632733, a training RMSE of 1.924860, and a training RMSLE of 0.159602, which are better than both polynomial and the baseline linear models, and the five cross validation confirms this assertion with a mean ross validated RMSE equal 1.925511, cross validated MAE equal 1.332366, mean cross validated R2 equal 0.632472, mean cross validated RMSLE was 0.159617. The polynomial model was close, kind of slightly worse, with a mean cross-validated RMSLE of 0.160674. The baseline linear model was definitely weaker, with a mean cross-validated RMSLE of 0.164939. Based on this body of evidence, we can say that the preferred non-linear model for this analysis was the natural cubic spline model. The plots also showed that whole_weight has a strong curved relationship with Rings. Length also showed a rise followed by a decline. Diameter curvature was more modest, but the relationship still did not appear perfectly linear (De Giosa et al., 2025).

(b) Interpretation of the Regression Models and Kaggle Submission Evidence¶

The interpretation of this analysis is pretty straightforward. The polynomial regression model is the easier of the two nonlinear models to interpret. In that model, C(sex)[T.I] had a negative and statistically significant coefficient, which indicates that, holding the other predictors constant, observations in the I category tended to have lower predicted Rings than the reference group. The coefficient for C(sex)[T.M] was not statistically significant, which suggests that after controlling for the other predictors, the distinction between that group and the reference group was weak in this model. The coefficient for I(length²) was negative and significant, which indicates that the effect of length was not simply increasing across the entire range. Instead, the relationship rose and then turned downward, which is consistent with the effect plot (James et al., 2023). The same pattern appeared for height, whole_weight, and shell_weight, where the squared terms were negative and statistically significant. That pattern suggests diminishing returns and curvature rather than a constant linear increase. The model also showed a strong negative linear coefficient for whole_weight_1 and a strong positive squared coefficient for I(whole_weight_12), which indicates a more complex curved response. Some terms, such as diameter, I(diameter2), and I(whole_weight_22), were not statistically significant, meaning their independent contribution was weaker once the other measurements were included. The VIF table showed extremely high multicollinearity for several predictors, especially diameter, length, and their squared terms. This is expected because raw size variables are highly related to one another, and squaring them creates even stronger dependence. As a result, the polynomial model is best interpreted through its overall fitted pattern rather than by treating each coefficient as a clean and isolated effect (Chesnaye et al., 2024). The spline model must be interpreted differently. Its basis coefficients were extremely large and not practically meaningful on their own. That is not unusual for spline basis representations. The spline effect plots showed that whole_weight had the clearest nonlinear association with Rings, with steep gains at lower and middle levels and flattening at the upper end. Length also showed a pronounced bend, while diameter displayed milder curvature. Because the model is additive, each smooth curve can be interpreted as the isolated contribution of one predictor while the others are held fixed. The supplied outputs show that the selected best model was the natural cubic spline model (De Giosa et al., 2025).

(c) Investigation of Assumptions and Interpretation of Findings¶

The first assumption issue examined was whether a simple linear structure was adequate. The comparison results strongly suggest that it was not. Both nonlinear models outperformed the baseline linear model on training fit and on cross-validated error. The ANOVA comparison between the linear and polynomial models was highly significant, which confirmed that adding nonlinear terms materially improved the model. The effect plots also showed clear bends in the relationships for length and whole weight. These findings support the conclusion that the linearity assumption was too restrictive for this problem and that nonlinear modeling was justified (Chesnaye et al., 2024). The second assumption issue was homoscedasticity, or constant error variance. Both nonlinear models showed evidence against this assumption. For the polynomial model, the Breusch Pagan F test p-value was 0.0. For the spline model, the Breusch Pagan F test p-value was also 0.0. These results indicate heteroscedasticity in both models. The residual versus fitted plots support the same conclusion. The spread of residuals was not constant across fitted values. The variability widened in some parts of the fitted range and narrowed in others. This means that prediction error changes across the response scale rather than remaining uniform. As a result, the constant variance assumption was violated (Chesnaye et al., 2024). The third assumption issue was residual normality. Once again, both nonlinear models failed this assumption. The Jarque-Bera p-values were 0.0 for both models, which means the residuals departed from normality. The residual histograms were centered near zero, but they were visibly right-skewed and had heavy tails. The QQ plots reinforced this conclusion. In both models, the residuals followed the reference line in the middle only loosely, but they bent away from the line in the tails, especially in the upper tail. That pattern indicates skewness and excess kurtosis. The reported skewness values of 1.521883 for the polynomial model and 1.512829 for the spline model, along with kurtosis values above 9, confirm that the residual distributions were not close to normal (Chesnaye et al., 2024).

The fourth assumption issue was the independence of errors. On this point, the results were favorable. The Durbin Watson statistic was 2.002191 for the polynomial model and 2.001348 for the spline model. Values near 2 suggest no strong evidence of autocorrelation. Therefore, based on the standard interpretation of Durbin-Watson, the independence assumption did not appear to be seriously violated in either nonlinear model (James et al., 2023). Another important issue was multicollinearity. The polynomial model showed extremely large VIF values. Diameter and length had VIF values above 15,000, while several other predictors and squared terms were also very large. This means that the predictors were strongly correlated with one another. In a body measurement dataset, this is not surprising because many size variables reflect overlapping biological dimensions. The spline model also showed huge and even infinite VIF values, but those should be interpreted differently. In spline regression, the basis functions are mathematically related by construction. Therefore, very large VIF values are expected and do not automatically imply that the model is unusable (De Giosa et al., 2025). The nonlinear models successfully addressed the problem of inadequate linearity and improved prediction accuracy. They did not fully satisfy the constant variance and normality assumptions, but they did show acceptable independence of errors. The polynomial model was easier to explain in direct algebraic terms, but it suffered from substantial multicollinearity. The natural cubic spline model was harder to interpret coefficient by coefficient, yet it captured the predictor response shapes more flexibly and produced the best predictive results. For that reason, the spline model is the strongest final choice for the Kaggle competition portion of the assignment (James et al., 2023).
